clinicalPearls: A seizure occurring with fever in children roughly 6 months to 5 years of age, without central nervous system infection or a metabolic cause, and not in a child with prior afebrile seizures.
Simple febrile seizures are generalised, last under 15 minutes, and do not recur within 24 hours; complex seizures are focal, prolonged, or recur within a day.
The diagnosis is clinical, and the main task is to exclude meningitis, encephalitis, and other acute causes of the fever.
Routine blood tests, neuroimaging, and EEG are not indicated for simple febrile seizures in an otherwise well child.
Lumbar puncture is considered when meningeal signs are present, in very young or incompletely immunised infants, or when the picture is atypical.
Most febrile seizures are brief and self-terminating; management centres on reassurance, identifying the febrile illness, and safety advice for parents.
Prolonged seizures are treated as status epilepticus with benzodiazepine-based abortive therapy and airway support.
Antipyretics improve comfort but do not reliably prevent recurrence, and daily prophylactic anticonvulsants are generally not recommended for simple febrile seizures.
reference.pathophysiology: Febrile seizures reflect the heightened seizure susceptibility of the developing brain when exposed to fever, likely mediated by fever-associated cytokines (such as interleukin-1 beta), the effect of raised temperature on neuronal excitability, and a genetic predisposition, as demonstrated by strong familial clustering. The rate of temperature rise and the immaturity of the young brain contribute, and in most children the tendency resolves with neurological maturation.
additionalDifferentials: Epilepsy with a coincidental febrile illness
Rigors or shivering mistaken for a seizure
additionalInvestigations: Assessment to identify and treat the source of fever
Blood glucose in any child who is drowsy or slow to recover
Lumbar puncture when CNS infection is suspected or the child is very young
Electrolytes only when clinically indicated (e.g. dehydration, atypical features)
EEG and neuroimaging reserved for complex or recurrent focal features or an abnormal neurological exam
redFlags: Signs of meningitis or encephalitis (neck stiffness, altered consciousness, bulging fontanelle)
Prolonged seizure or febrile status epilepticus
Focal features, or focal neurological deficit after the seizure
Failure to return to baseline alertness within a reasonable period
Seizure outside the typical age range or in an unwell, toxic-appearing child
reference.prognosis: The outlook is excellent: most children have normal development and neurological outcome, though about a third experience a recurrence, and the increase in later epilepsy risk is small for simple febrile seizures.
pitfalls: Assuming fever excludes meningitis and skipping evaluation in a young or unwell infant
Over-investigating a well child after a simple febrile seizure
Reassuring families that antipyretics prevent recurrence
Starting long-term anticonvulsants for simple febrile seizures unnecessarily
management: Manage the acute seizure with airway protection and positioning, giving benzodiazepine rescue therapy only for a prolonged or ongoing seizure
Identify and treat the underlying febrile illness, using antipyretics such as paracetamol or ibuprofen for the child's comfort
Exclude central nervous system infection clinically, performing lumbar puncture when meningeal signs are present, in very young or incompletely immunised infants, or when the picture is atypical
Avoid routine bloods, neuroimaging and EEG in a simple febrile seizure in an otherwise well child, reserving them for complex, focal or recurrent features
Provide parental reassurance and safety advice, including first-aid seizure management and when to seek urgent help
Reserve referral to paediatric neurology for complex, atypical or recurrent seizures or an abnormal neurological examination
